Field surveys of Labeo coubie in the Niger River basin have provided detailed measurements of somatic growth and reproductive development. The maximum recorded total length for this African cyprinid is 75 cm [Li = 75 cm], a value consistent with the upper size range observed among large-bodied members of the genus. Reproductive maturation, as indicated by the onset of gonadal recrudescence, occurs at a considerably smaller body size; individuals typically attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of 22 cm [Lp = 22 cm]. This marked difference between size at puberty and ultimate size suggests a prolonged period of somatic growth following the onset of reproductive capability. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated at 119.5 grams [Wwp = 119.5 grams], derived from length-weight regressions specific to this species. In contrast, the asymptotic body mass, representing the maximum wet weight achieved by fully grown adults, is approximately 4,900 grams [Wwi = approximately 4,900 grams], reflecting the substantial increase in mass that accompanies the extended growth phase characteristic of this potamodromous fish.

Embryonic and early larval development in Labeo coubie proceeds rapidly under stable thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], hatching occurs approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days] after fertilisation, a developmental tempo comparable to that reported for other tropical cyprinids with similarly small pelagic eggs. The incubation duration at this temperature is relatively brief, facilitating high rates of early survival in floodplain spawning habitats where water temperatures are consistently elevated during the monsoon season. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are diminutive, with an initial wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0005 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0005 grams]. This minute mass, corresponding to an egg diameter of roughly 1 mm, places the species among the smaller-egged cyprinids and reflects a life-history strategy emphasising high fecundity over per-offspring investment. The rapid depletion of endogenous yolk reserves soon after eclosion drives the transition to exogenous feeding within a few days post-hatching.

The reproductive output of Labeo coubie is characterised by high fecundity and the production of multiple batches of eggs during the extended spawning season. Females typically release approximately 334 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 334 eggs per spawning event] during peak reproductive activity, sustained over the course of the breeding period. This per-event fecundity represents a substantial reproductive allocation consistent with the species' iteroparous life cycle. Under the thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] that prevails in its floodplain nursery habitats, the maximum daily reproductive rate is achieved, with individuals capable of generating around 122,000 eggs over a 365-day reproductive cycle [N_R_i = around 122,000 eggs over a 365-day reproductive cycle]. This high output is facilitated by the continuous recruitment of vitellogenic oocytes and the species' ability to capitalise on seasonally abundant food resources. Such elevated fecundity is typical of large-bodied, long-lived cyprinids that experience variable juvenile survival in unpredictable riverine environments.

Longevity records for Labeo coubie indicate a comparatively extended lifespan relative to many other African cyprinid species. At a sustained water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], individuals have been documented to survive for up to 10 years [am = up to 10 years] under natural conditions, a longevity comparable to other large-bodied cyprinids in West African rivers. This maximum lifespan is consistent with the species' asymptotic body size and its slow pace of life, which includes delayed maturity and a protracted reproductive window. When expressed in days, this longevity equates to approximately 3,650 days [am = approximately 3,650 days], a span that enables multiple spawning seasons across an individual's lifetime at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Such longevity is advantageous in the variable hydrological regimes of West African rivers, where interannual fluctuations in flooding extent and duration can strongly influence recruitment success. The ability to reproduce over several consecutive years buffers the population against years of poor reproductive conditions.

Comparative metabolic and life-history data further contextualise the growth trajectory of Labeo coubie. The maximum observed body length of 75 cm [Li = 75 cm] places this species among the largest cyprinids in the region, comparable in ultimate size to certain Labeo congeners from the Congo Basin. The mass increment from the pubertal weight of 119.5 grams [Wwp = 119.5 grams] to the adult asymptotic weight of 4,900 grams [Wwi = 4,900 grams] represents a more than forty-fold increase, underscoring the substantial energy allocation devoted to somatic growth during the subadult phase. This pattern aligns with the general teleost life-history continuum, where species with larger ultimate body sizes tend to exhibit delayed maturation and extended growth periods. Field mark-recapture studies have shown that growth rates remain relatively high until individuals approach the asymptotic length, after which reproductive investment presumably dominates the energy budget. The species' life-history strategy, combining high fecundity and moderate longevity, is well suited to the seasonal and often unpredictable floodplain ecosystems it inhabits.
